## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Consensus
Consensus is a research paper search engine: relevance-ranked semantic search over 400M+ peer-reviewed papers (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, PubMed). Use the `search` tool to look up papers for a scientific query; it takes plain-language queries and returns ranked paper records. When presenting search results, you MUST cite papers inline using their numbered references from the tool result (e.g. [1], [2], [3]). When discussing findings, always attribute them to specific papers: 'Caffeine improves endurance performance [1] and reduces perceived exertion [3].' At the end of your response, list all cited papers as numbered references with their titles hyperlinked to the URLs from the tool result: [1] [Paper Title](url) (Authors, Year, Journal, Citations). Use the exact paper URLs from the tool result — do not modify, shorten, or regenerate them. Do not omit paper links or summarize results without citing specific papers. IMPORTANT: At the END of your response, you MUST include the sign-up, upgrade, or usage message from the tool result word-for-word. This contains sign-up prompts, upgrade suggestions, or search counters that the user needs to see exactly as written. Do not omit, shorten, or rephrase it. Batch at most 3 search calls at a time to avoid rate limits. For a broad request (a review, screening, finding everything on a topic), make one search with a large page_size rather than many narrower searches. If you receive a rate limit error, wait 30 seconds before retrying. Do NOT apply search filters (year_min, year_max, study_types, domain, human, sample_size_min, sjr_max, controlled, sjr_min, citation_min, open_access, country) unless the user explicitly requests them or clearly expresses intent to narrow results. If the user asks a research question without mentioning filtering criteria, call search with only the query parameter.

## claude.ai Context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, porting code between libraries, platforms, or SQL dialects, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, debugging, or reviewing code that does not depend on a library or platform API, or general programming concepts.

## claude.ai Slack
Before posting a new message to a Slack channel the user didn't name, read its topic and description with slack_search_channels, and if they say that kind of message belongs elsewhere, tell the user instead of posting.

## claude.ai Typefully - Social Media Scheduler
Create, schedule, and publish social media posts with Typefully across X/Twitter, LinkedIn, Threads, Bluesky, Mastodon, and Substack, and read post analytics.

- superpowers:writing-plans: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code
- superpowers:writing-skills: Use when creating new skills, editing existing skills, or verifying skills work before deployment

# CLAUDE.md — wol-sok-mono

Angular + Nx monorepo. Read this before touching anything.

## Stack

- **Angular 20** — standalone components, zoneless change detection, Signals, `@if`/`@for`/`@switch` control flow
- **Nx 23** — monorepo orchestration, caching, affected commands
- **TypeScript 5.9** — strict mode
- **Build**: Vite (Analog/Vitest apps), Webpack + Module Federation (angular-examples)
- **Testing**: Jest (most unit tests), Vitest (Vite projects), Playwright (E2E)
- **Lint / Format**: oxlint (`.oxlintrc.json`, targets inferred by `@nx/oxlint`), angular-eslint for templates only (`eslint.config.mjs`, target `lint-templates`) and oxfmt (`.oxfmtrc.json`, driven by `nx format`)
- **UI**: Angular Material + CDK everywhere (no custom primitives if AM covers it)
- **State**: Angular Signals (local/sync), RxJS (async), NgRx Signal Store (bacteria game), Akita/Elf (older app-wide stores)
- **Backend**: Firebase (Hosting, Auth, DB), AWS CDK (S3/CloudFront infra)
- **Package manager**: npm (use `npm ci`, never yarn/pnpm)

## Project Layout

```
apps/                   # Deployable apps
  angular-examples/     # Main showcase (Webpack + Module Federation)
  pacetrainer/          # Pace trainer (Vite + Analog.js)
  rollapolla-analog/    # Analog.js SSR demo
  *-remote/             # Module Federation remotes
  *-cdk/                # AWS CDK infra stacks
  bacteria-wars-android/ # Android app (Gradle, Trusted Web Activity)
libs/
  features/             # Domain features (can use shared + utils + ui-kit)
  shared/               # Cross-cutting concerns (can use utils)
  utils/                # Pure utilities (minimal deps)
  ui-kit/               # Reusable UI components
  public/               # Published npm packages (e.g. @wolsok/thanos)
  fib-wasm/             # WebAssembly modules
  test-helper/          # Testing utilities
tools/                  # Build/deploy node scripts
docs/                   # Architecture, testing, getting-started docs
```

## Essential Commands

```bash
# Install
npm ci

# Serve
npx nx serve pacetrainer
npx nx serve angular-examples

# Build
npx nx build <project> [--configuration production]

# Test
npx nx test <project>
npx nx run <project>:e2e

# Lint (always --fix)
npx nx lint <project> --fix            # oxlint
npx nx lint-templates <project> --fix  # angular-eslint template rules
npm run lint                          # all projects, both targets

# Format (REQUIRED before committing)
npx nx format:write

# Affected only (prefer in CI / large PRs)
npx nx affected -t build,test,lint,lint-templates

# Dependency graph
npx nx graph
```

## Engineering Principles (mandatory)

Long-term, strategic software engineering is required. A change that works but leaves the code harder to change is not done.

- **Improve the codebase with every feature and bug fix.** Leave the code you touch cleaner than you found it: extract duplication, split oversized files/functions/components, fix misleading names, remove dead code, and add missing tests around what you changed.
- **Fix root causes, not symptoms.** No workarounds or one-off special cases when the underlying design is the problem; fix the design.
- **Stay modular.** Small, focused units with one responsibility and narrow interfaces. Put logic in the right `libs/` layer (see Dependency Constraints) instead of growing app code; keep domain logic out of components and in testable services/stores/pure functions.
- **Clean Code is the standard.** Intention-revealing names, small functions, no magic values, no deep nesting, no copy-paste, single level of abstraction per function, explicit error handling.
- **Easy to maintain beats clever.** Prefer simple, readable code a newcomer can follow over terse or tricky solutions.
- **Scope of cleanup:** improvements to the code your change touches belong in the same PR. A larger refactor that the change exposes but doesn't need goes in its own PR (or an issue), so each PR stays reviewable.

## Coding Rules

1. **Standalone components only** — no NgModules
2. **Zoneless change detection** — never add `zone.js` imports or zone-dependent patterns
3. **Signals for state** — prefer `signal()`/`computed()`/`effect()` over manual subscriptions where possible
4. **OnPush everywhere** — `changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`
5. **Angular Material** — use AM components consistently; don't roll custom UI that AM already covers
   - Exception (pacetrainer): the countdown ring (`pace-countdown-circle`) is a custom SVG, since `mat-progress-spinner` has no track ring
6. **Modern control flow** — `@if`, `@for`, `@switch` (not `*ngIf`, `*ngFor`, `*ngSwitch`)
7. **2-space indentation**, kebab-case filenames, `*.spec.ts` for tests
8. **Explicit `public`/`private`** in class members
9. **Strongly typed** — avoid `any`; use proper generics

## Linting & Formatting

- One workspace-wide `.oxlintrc.json`; there are no per-project lint configs. Add project-specific rules through `overrides` with a `files` glob.
- Type-aware linting is on (`options.typeAware`, backed by `oxlint-tsgolint`). It reads each project's `tsconfig.json` with TypeScript 7 semantics: no `baseUrl`, `paths` relative to `tsconfig.base.json` (`./libs/...`), and no `moduleResolution: node`/`node10`. Keep new tsconfigs on that layout or lint reports `tsconfig-error`.
- `@nx/enforce-module-boundaries` runs inside oxlint through the `@nx/oxlint/boundaries-plugin` bridge; tag constraints live in `.oxlintrc.json`.
- oxlint only lints JS/TS. Angular templates are covered by a second, template-only ESLint setup: the root `eslint.config.mjs` (angular-eslint template rules for `.html` and inline templates, plus the per-project component/directive selector prefixes) is inferred as the `lint-templates` target by `@nx/eslint/plugin`. New Angular projects get their selector prefix added to `selectorPrefixes` in that file. The JSON-based `@nx/dependency-checks` rule is gone; keep package.json deps correct by hand.
- `nx format:write` / `nx format:check` run oxfmt (HTML, SCSS, Markdown and YAML are formatted through its Prettier-backed path).

## Dependency Constraints

```
apps        → features, shared, utils, ui-kit
features    → shared, utils, ui-kit
shared      → utils
utils       → (minimal external deps only)
public      → (own deps only, published packages)
```

Do not create circular dependencies. Run `npx nx graph` to verify.

## Target Policy

- Root `.browserslistrc` and `tsconfig.base.json` govern everything — apps/libs inherit.
- **Do not bump targets in `libs/public/*`** — published packages, held back for consumer compat.
- **`apps/*-cdk` use `target: "ESNext"`** intentionally (Node runtime) — exclude from browser-target changes.

## Native Federation

- `angular-examples` is the shell, remotes are `fourier-analysis-remote`, `bacteria-game-remote`, `shader-examples-remote`.
- Shared setup lives in `tools/federation/workspace-federation.js`; each app's `federation.config.js` only adds its name and `exposes`. A package skipped in one app must be skipped in all of them, or the shell and a remote disagree about the import map. The game lib's secondary entries (`engine`, `admin-kit`, `watch`) are skipped there with the lib.
- `exposes` paths resolve from the workspace root (`./apps/<app>/src/...`), not the project root.
- **Nothing but the exposed module belongs in `src/app/remote-entry/`.** Native Federation maps the whole _directory_ of an exposed file to the remote's public name, so a sibling file imported with a static `import` from outside that folder is rewritten to `<remote>/Routes` and its exports vanish at runtime. That is why each remote's bootstrap component sits in `src/app/`, not next to `entry.routes.ts`.
- A remote also has to run standalone (its own e2e serves it that way), so check both: loaded through the shell _and_ opened on its own port.
- Remotes are listed in `apps/angular-examples/src/assets/federation.manifest.json` (dev) and `federation.manifest.prod.json` (prod).
- Each app has an `esbuild` target (`@angular/build:application`) wrapped by a `build`/`serve` target from `@angular-architects/native-federation`. Change build options on `esbuild`.
- `bacteria-game-remote` runs on Firebase Hosting (`firebase.bacteria-game-remote.json`, site `bacteria-wars`, domain `bacteria-wars.wolsok.de`), deployed by its `deploy` target together with the Firestore and Realtime Database rules. The shell's prod manifest loads the remote from there, and the shell reloads once when a navigation fails on a remote bundle a release replaced (`core/reload-on-stale-bundle.ts`). The old domain `bacteria-game.wolsok.de` is gone; `bacteria-game-remote-cdk` (stack `BacteriaGame`) only holds the new domain's CNAME, whose construct id must stay as it is.
- The game's legal pages live in `bacteria-game-remote`, not the lib: `/privacy` and `/impressum` (`src/app/privacy`, `src/app/impressum`, sharing `src/app/legal/`). Both name the provider from `SITE_OWNER` (`@wolsok/shared-legal`, `libs/shared/legal`: name, email, postal address, VAT ID), shown by its `SiteOwnerComponent` (`<wolsok-site-owner>`), as on RollaPolla's and wolsok.de's `/privacy` and `/impressum`, which also fills `siteOwner` in the support options for the footer's copyright line. The game lib's `support/` folder links to the pages from the footer under the main menu (the route paths are the lib's `legal-links.ts`, used by `app.routes.ts`) and offers the Android app or the PWA in a banner (`InstallOffer`), both only where `provideGameSupport` is set up: on the game's own site, never in the shell.
- The owner's admin area (ADR 0012) is the lib `feat-lazy-bacteria-wars-admin` (tag `feature:admin`, prefix `feat-lazy-bac-admin`), loaded by `/admin` in `bacteria-game-remote`'s `app.routes.ts` only, never through the exposed routes. It takes from the game only `@wolsok/feat-lazy-bac-game/admin-kit`, has texts of its own in English and German, and must stay out of what every visitor loads: the remote's production `build` ends with `tools/bacteria-game/check-lazy-admin.mjs`, which fails when the admin's sources reach `main`, the polyfills or `Routes`.
- Exception: `bacteria-game-remote` is also a standalone PWA. Its federation build is `build-federation`; `build` then reruns `ngsw-config`, since the federation builder writes its files after Angular has hashed the output into `ngsw.json`.
- Error reports go to Sentry (org `wolsok`): the shell to `angular-examples` (`bootstrap.ts`, `core/core.module.ts`), the game to `bacteria-wars`, started only by the remote's standalone `bootstrap.ts` and `app.config.ts` (`src/app/error-reports/`), never by the lib or the exposed routes, and only where the environment has a `sentry` block (`environment.prod.ts`). The SDK is imported dynamically (`import()` in `error-reports.ts`), so it stays off the start's path; errors from before it loaded wait for it. Import it nowhere else but as a type. Errors only and no personal data (owner's decision of 2026-10-26): no tracing, Replay or sessions, `dataCollection.userInfo: false`, and `scrub.ts` drops the user, strips query, hash (`#friend=…`) and id-like tokens, and the attributes of click breadcrumbs (avatars name players in `aria-label` and `alt`). `@sentry/angular` is skipped in `workspace-federation.js`, so each app bundles its own copy. The release is `bacteria-wars@v<version.json>`, created by `.github/actions/create-release`; a change to what is sent goes into the privacy policy (section 10) too.
- Fonts and icons are self-hosted: each app's global `styles.scss` imports the Fontsource faces (latin subsets) and `material-icons/iconfont/filled.css`, and nothing loads from Google Fonts (Angular's font inlining fetched them at build time, which failed the release build, and Google would get every visitor's IP). The shell imports the game's faces too (Atkinson Hyperlegible, Bricolage Grotesque, Cookie), since only the remote's JavaScript reaches it. The game's PWA caches them as `/media/**`.
- `nx serve angular-examples` only serves the shell. Use `nx run angular-examples:serve-all` to boot the shell plus all remotes (ports 4200-4203).

## Cloud Functions (Bacteria Wars)

- `apps/bacteria-wars-functions` is the game's server code (ADR 0011, 0012): 2nd-gen functions, codebase `bacteria` in `firebase.bacteria-game-remote.json`, region `REGION` in `src/config.ts` (the Firestore location of `bacteria-wars`). It takes the engine from `@wolsok/feat-lazy-bac-game/engine` and bundles it (`@nx/esbuild`, ESM, `thirdParty: false`); `firebase-admin` and `firebase-functions` stay external, at the versions in the app's own `package.json`, which a spec keeps equal to the workspace's.
- The client never calls a function: it writes command documents (`replaySubmissions`, `replayCommands`) that triggers process. Triggers run with retries off and are idempotent (`create()` or a transaction checks first).
- The boards (`src/boards/`) are written by functions only: entries carry no uid (`boardMembers/{uid}.entryIds` maps them), `rebuildTop` alone writes a board's top document, and every composite query has its index checked by `indexes.spec.ts` against `firestore.indexes.json`, since the emulator enforces none.
- `test` runs the pure specs; `test-emulator` runs `*.emulator.ts` against the Firestore emulator on ports of its own (`emulator.json`). The game's rules are tested the same way in `apps/bacteria-game-remote/rules-test` (`bacteria-game-remote:test-emulator`). CI runs both targets.
- Errors go to the Sentry project `bacteria-wars-functions` (`src/error-reports.ts`, DSN `SENTRY_DSN` in `src/config.ts`): `main.ts` calls `initErrorReports()`, which starts `@sentry/node` only in a deployed function (`K_SERVICE` set, not the emulator or Jest), and wraps every exported handler in `withSentry(handler)`, which captures, waits for `flush` and rethrows, so retries stay as they were. A new function gets the wrapper too; handler modules stay free of Sentry. `@sentry/node` is external and in the app's `package.json` at the workspace's version (`package-json.spec.ts`).
- Handler modules import `firebase-functions/logger`, not `firebase-functions`: the root export loads the admin auth stack, which Jest on Node 22 cannot require.
- Re-running a replay (`boards/verify.ts`) costs real CPU: `gpu-int`, the only ruleset ranked attempts take, plays at about 7 ms a tick on `IntSimulation`, so a 10-minute match takes minutes. Specs never replay whole matches: `verifyDailySlice` takes the verifier as a parameter, and `verify.spec.ts` mocks `playReplay`. Firestore holds no arrays in arrays; flatten what a function stores.
- `hourly` (`boards/hourly.ts`) is exported only with `HOURLY_ON` in `src/config.ts`; set it to `false` to take it out of a deploy.
- `featureBest` (`gallery/feature-best.ts`, the gallery's daily pick into `publicReplays`) is exported only with `FEATURE_BEST_ON` in `src/config.ts`, on since the gallery's pages and the Replays view of `/admin` shipped (ADR 0011 rollout step 6); set it to `false` to take it out of a deploy.
- Account deletion erases the player's data (ADR 0012, owner's decisions of 2026-10-26) through three `auth.user().onDelete` triggers: `deletePlayerBoards` (`admin/accounts.ts`: boards, bans, audit, count), `deletePlayerData` (`social/delete-player.ts`: `players/{uid}/**`, profile, the player in other players' lists, queue, open rooms, invites, presence and both mirrors) and `deletePlayerReplays`, which no longer deletes replays: `replays/forget.ts` takes the uid out of `players`, seats, `optOut` and `reports`, and the replay stays for the statistics until its `expireAt` (none while still public). It deletes the player's pending `replaySubmissions` and `replayCommands` first; `acceptReplay` reads its submission in its slot and store transactions and drops one that is gone (`withdrawn`), so taking the slot marks the submission (`slotTaken`) rather than deleting it. A new collection keyed by uid, or one that names a uid in a field, gets its erasing there too. Keep `erasePlayer` (`admin/erase.ts`) calling all three parts.
- `guestCleanup` (`admin/guests.ts`, daily at 03:41 UTC) deletes guest accounts (no provider) unused for `GUEST_IDLE_DAYS` (90); exported only with `GUEST_CLEANUP_ON`, on together with the friends-only status rule, which ships only after "Mirror friend lists" (`presence.backfill`) has run once in production. Auth's bulk `deleteUsers` fires no `onDelete`, so it runs `erasePlayer` for each guest first and deletes the account only once that succeeded. It lowers `stats/accounts` once a batch by the decrements its erases claimed (`accountCounted` cleared in a transaction, so each account counts down once), never once a guest.
- The friend lists are mirrored into the Realtime Database by `mirrorFriend` and `mirrorRequest` (`social/mirror.ts`): `statusReaders/{owner}/{reader}` (for the coming friends-only read rule of `status/{owner}`) and `listedBy/{uid}/{owner}/{friends|requests}` (where the deletion finds the player in others' lists). Functions only: the database rules close both to clients. Both triggers retry; each re-reads the entry after its write and writes again if it changed, so out-of-order events end right. Ids the Realtime Database takes as no key (`isRealtimeKey` in `admin/realtime.ts`) are skipped everywhere, and the Firestore rules take only uid-shaped ids in `friends`, `requests` and `challenges`. The admin command `presence.backfill` adds what is missing and removes entries without a list entry.
- The player's replay command `forget` ("Delete" in "My matches", `replays/forget.ts`) takes them out of the replay and its public copies; allowed while banned, like every deletion, and refused (`ranking`) while the boards may still rank the match, an online match still `waiting` for its second report included (`stillRanking` in `replays/forget-plan.ts`).
- Its `deploy` target (`firebase deploy --config=firebase.bacteria-game-remote.json --only functions:bacteria --force`) calls the Firebase CLI itself, not `nx run bacteria-game-remote:firebase`: the game's hosting deploy runs that task in the same release, and the second, nested run of it failed every functions deploy. It runs in the `non-cdk` leg of `deploy.yml` whenever a release affects the app, which includes every change to the game lib (`feat-lazy-bacteria-game`), since the app imports its engine. `--force` deletes functions of the `bacteria` codebase that are gone from `main.ts`, so taking a function out of the exports takes it out of production. The game's hosting deploy leaves the functions alone (`--only hosting,firestore,database`).
- Every Firebase `predeploy` that runs `npm install` for a function (`firebase.bacteria-game-remote.json`, `firebase.pacetrainer.json`, `firebase.rollapolla-analog.json`) passes `--legacy-peer-deps=false`: deploys run inside `npx nx`, which exports the root `.npmrc` as `npm_config_legacy_peer_deps=true`, and the lock written that way lacks required peers, so Cloud Build's `npm ci` refuses it (`Missing: … from lock file`). A spec in each app keeps the flag (`package-json.spec.ts`, `firebase-deploy.spec.ts`); a new function config gets both.

**Keep the portfolio in sync, in the same PR as the sitemap.** `apps/portfolio/src/app/projects.ts` lists every app, every `angular-examples` page worth showing (`EXPERIMENTS`) and every published package (`PACKAGES`); a change that adds, renames, removes or noticeably changes one updates its entry too (name, description, tech, links). The portfolio's `app.component.spec.ts` fails when a link points to an `angular-examples` page its sitemap doesn't list.

- **rollapolla-analog**: `/sitemap.xml` is a Nitro route (`src/server/routes/sitemap.xml.ts`, URLs from `src/server/sitemap/sitemap.ts`). A new indexable page goes into `sitemapUrls`. `/privacy` (`pages/privacy.page.html`) is the privacy policy, linked from the footer and the consent banner: a new third party, collection or consent purpose goes into it in the same change. `/impressum` (`pages/impressum.page.html`, linked from the footer) is the legal notice, also naming the Digital Services Act's point of contact. Every page sets its tags through `usePageTags` / `useNoindexPage` in `src/app/pages/site-tags.ts`: its own title, description and canonical URL, and `noindex` for personal pages. - **angular-examples**: `src/sitemap.xml` is kept by hand. It lists every route in `APP_ROUTES`, or its visible tabs when the route redirects to one, since the canonical URL is the URL after the redirect. Every main route needs a `data.description`. `seo.service.spec.ts` checks both: update it together with the sitemap.
- **portfolio** (`wolsok.de`): prerendered (`outputMode: static`), so each route is a page of its own. `public/sitemap.xml` is kept by hand and lists every route in `app.routes.ts` (`app.component.spec.ts` checks it); each route sets `data.title` and `data.description` in both languages, `SeoService` sets title, canonical and Open Graph tags for the active language. A new project goes into `src/app/projects.ts`. `public/ads.txt` and the AdSense tags in `index.html` belong to AdSense; keep them. `portfolio-cdk` uploads each prerendered page a second time under its bare path, because CloudFront serves no folder index.
  - The site speaks English and German at runtime (`src/app/i18n/`: `I18nService`, `texts.en.ts` with `texts.de.ts` owing it every key, `Localized` values in the data) and is prerendered in English; a German browser switches after hydration, the choice is kept in `localStorage`. The theme (`src/app/theme/`) follows the system through `color-scheme: light dark` and `light-dark()` in `styles.scss`; a choice pins `data-theme`, which a script in `index.html` restores before the first paint.

  - `/career` (`src/app/career/`) is the qualification profile: its data in `career.data.ts` is a typed, bilingual copy of the newest profile in Google Drive, named by `CAREER_SOURCE`. A monthly scheduled Claude task updates it as `docs/agents/career-update.md` says; `career.spec.ts` checks the data, the build's budgets its size.
- **bacteria-game-remote** (`bacteria-wars.wolsok.de`): `src/sitemap.xml` and `src/robots.txt` are kept by hand and shipped as assets. The sitemap lists the game and every page route in `app.routes.ts` (`sitemap.spec.ts` checks it); the legal pages set their tags through `legal/legal-page.ts`, with the origin from the lib's `GAME_SITE_URL`. The public replay pages (`/replays`, `/replays/{id}`) are no SPA routes: Hosting rewrites `/replays` and `/replays/**` to the `publicSite` function (`apps/bacteria-wars-functions/src/site/`), which renders their tags itself and serves their own sitemap, `/replays/sitemap.xml` (both languages, with `hreflang` alternates), listed in `robots.txt` beside the game's (`site/hosting.spec.ts` checks the rewrites and their cache headers, `sitemap.spec.ts` that line). ## Testing

- **Unit (Jest)**: colocated as `<file>.spec.ts`; mock external services; keep fast and deterministic
- **Unit (Vitest)**: used in Vite-based projects (check `project.json` for the `@nx/vitest` plugin / `@nx/vitest:test` executor)
- **E2E (Playwright)**: in `apps/<app>/e2e/`; page objects in `e2e/pos/`, fixtures in `e2e/fixtures/`
  - Start every `webServer` through an Nx target (`npx nx serve <app>`, `npx nx run <app>:<target>` for a `continuous` target) with `reuseExistingServer: true`. Only then does `@nx/playwright` make the atomized `e2e-ci--*` tasks depend on those servers and wait for them, so several spec files on one Nx Cloud worker share them. A server Playwright starts itself clashes with the next spec file on the same worker (see `rollapolla-analog`). A static server (`@nx/web:file-server`) serves `staticFilePath` and `dependsOn: ["build"]` with `watch: false`, not a `buildTarget`: with `buildTarget` it runs a nested `nx build`, which Nx refuses as a recursive task invocation inside a shared run. Exception for now: `angular-examples` (the federation shell, one spec file) still lets Playwright start its server in CI; with the inferred serve dependency its page did not render on the Nx Cloud workers, while it passed locally.
- **GPU cross-check (Playwright, no server)**: `libs/features/lazy/bacteria-game/playwright.config.ts` runs the deterministic simulation's integer shaders on SwiftShader against the TypeScript reference, tick by tick (`gpu-crosscheck/`, ADR 0015). It is inferred as the lib's `e2e-ci--*` target, so `nx affected` runs it in CI. The goldens in `golden-gpu-int.json` are regenerated whenever the scenarios, the reference or the hash change; a change to what the passes compute also needs a `BALANCE_VERSION` bump, a scenario change does not; `golden.spec.ts` (Jest) recomputes them from the reference. The same check plays whole matches through the game's `GpuSimulation` (`SIM_SCENARIOS`) against `golden-gpu-sim.json`, which `sim-golden.spec.ts` keeps equal to `IntSimulation`, and runs the on-device self-test; its own hashes are `SELF_TEST_GOLDEN` (`state/gpu-int/self-test-golden.ts`, with `GPU_SELF_TEST_VERSION` bumped on every change), kept in step by `self-test-golden.spec.ts`. `golden-replay.spec.ts` keeps a result of `golden-replay.json` per `BALANCE_VERSION` for each ruleset: `cpu` on `BacteriaSimulation`, `gpu-int` on `IntSimulation`
- **Plugin E2E (Jest)**: `apps/nx-aws-cdk-v2-e2e` exercises `@wolsok/nx-aws-cdk-v2` in a generated throwaway workspace. Its target is `e2e` (not `e2e-ci`), so CI does not run it — run `npx nx e2e nx-aws-cdk-v2-e2e` by hand after changing the plugin
- Run `npx nx affected -t test` before pushing

## Performance Gates

Planned and phased in [ADR 0014](docs/adr/0014-performance-gates-in-ci.md); this section says what is in place. Keep it current with each phase.

- **In place, blocking** (phase 1): Angular budgets on the `production` configuration of each Angular app's `esbuild` target (`portfolio`: `build`), measured through the federation build as CI runs it. CI's `build -c=ci` falls back to `production`, so they run on every affected build and block it. Each holds a `baseline` (measured on 2026-10-26, 1 kB = 1000 bytes as Angular counts):
  - `anyScript` (the largest single script, the game's chunk in `bacteria-game-remote`) and `allScript` (all scripts, initial and lazy): warning +5%, error +10%.
  - `initial`: warning +10%, error +20%.
  - `anyComponentStyle` as before (warning 6 kB, error 8 kB in the game's apps), with no warning left: a stylesheet near the limit gives a part of its component a component of its own (the HUD bar `hud-bar.component.ts`, the training's `menu/mission-list.component.ts`) or groups rules it repeats, rather than raising the limit.
  - pacetrainer and rollapolla-analog build with Vite (Analog) and have no Angular budgets.
- **In place, report-only** (phase 2, since 2026-10-27, blocking after two weeks): the `perf` target on `feat-lazy-bacteria-game` runs `tools/perf/engine-bench.mjs`, which bundles `engine.ts` with esbuild and plays fixed replays (the golden replay on `cpu` and `gpu-int`, and `tools/perf/fixtures/expanse-heavy.json`), comparing each one's median time as a ratio to a calibration loop against `tools/perf/engine-baseline.json`: warns above +10%, fails above +20%, asks for a lower baseline below −10%, and fails when a replay plays differently (checksum, ticks, outcome), no longer parses, or the baseline was measured on another Node major than `.nvmrc`'s (V8 optimises differently, so its ratios don't compare). It is cached, runs alone on its worker (`parallelism: false`), takes about 1.5 minutes and writes its table into the job summary. `--report-only` keeps it from failing until the two weeks are over; the baseline holds the CI workers' ratios on Node 24 (they don't carry over between machines, and not even between all CI workers: one run measured 40-50% above the others, so the report names the CPU, and the two weeks decide whether baselines go per CPU model), so a new baseline (a `perf(feat-lazy-bacteria-game): ...` commit of its own, also due when `BALANCE_VERSION` changes the checksums) takes its ratios from the `perf` output of a CI run; `--update` writes the local machine's, useful only for the checksums.
- **In place, report-only** (phase 3, since 2026-10-27): `apps/bacteria-game-remote/e2e/perf.spec.ts` (Chromium only) plays up to 20 s (at least 8) of a campaign match against the computer on the CPU simulation (`?sim=cpu`), with `Math.random` pinned to a seed by an init script, and reports the frame interval (p50, p95, max), long tasks and the engine's time per tick, each also as a ratio to the calibration loop run in the page. The tick time comes from the game's probe (`state/perf-probe.ts`): the spec puts `window.__bacteriaPerfProbe` on the page before it loads, and `GameStateService.advance` times each tick only then; the game never creates it. The table goes to the log (and the job summary where `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` is set), the numbers into the attachment `frame-time.json`; it fails only when nothing was measured. On SwiftShader the frames take about 67 ms and a tick about 2.5 ms: the painting, not the engine, sets the pace there.
- **In place, report-only** (phase 4, since 2026-10-27): Lighthouse CI (`@lhci/cli`) as a `lighthouse` target on `portfolio` (every prerendered route, listed in its `lighthouse.json`, which `app.component.spec.ts` keeps equal to `app.routes.ts`), `angular-examples` (`/`) and `rollapolla-analog` (`/`, `/polls`), each after its `build`, cached, alone on its worker. `tools/perf/lighthouse-run.mjs <app>` runs `lhci autorun` on Playwright's Chrome (`CHROME_PATH` wins where set), with the app's `apps/<app>/lighthouse.json` (what to serve, which pages) and the shared settings it holds itself: 3 runs per page, mobile defaults, warnings only (LCP 2.5 s, TBT 200 ms, CLS 0.1, 1.6 MB), uploaded to temporary public storage in CI (links in the log), `.lighthouseci/` elsewhere. rollapolla's build is Nitro's `firebase` preset, which listens nowhere: `tools/perf/serve-firebase-function.mjs` serves its public folder and hands every other path to the exported function, as Hosting does; its SSR reads the real project's public polls. The public replay pages of the game (a Cloud Function behind Hosting) are not measured yet.
- **Rules**:
  - A failing gate is fixed in the code, not by raising the limit. Raise a budget or baseline only for growth you want, in its own `perf(<project>): ...` commit, with what grew, by how much and why in the PR body. Lower it when a gate reports a gain.
  - Don't compare absolute milliseconds from CI: the Nx Cloud workers are shared and vary. Runtime gates compare against a calibration loop run in the same process.

```
  rollapolla-analog/    # Analog.js SSR demo

libs/
  features/             # Domain features (can use shared + utils + ui-kit)
  shared/               # Cross-cutting concerns (can use utils)
  utils/                # Pure utilities (minimal deps)
  ui-kit/               # Reusable UI components
  public/               # Published npm packages (e.g. @wolsok/thanos)
  fib-wasm/             # WebAssembly modules
  test-helper/          # Testing utilities
tools/                  # Build/deploy node scripts
docs/                   # Architecture, testing, getting-started docs
```

## Essential Commands

```bash
# Install
npm ci

# Serve
npx nx serve pacetrainer
npx nx serve angular-examples

# Build
npx nx build <project> [--configuration production]

# Test
npx nx test <project>
npx nx run <project>:e2e

# Lint (always --fix)
npx nx lint <project> --fix            # oxlint
npx nx lint-templates <project> --fix  # angular-eslint template rules
npm run lint                          # all projects, both targets

# Format (REQUIRED before committing)
npx nx format:write

# Affected only (prefer in CI / large PRs)
npx nx affected -t build,test,lint,lint-templates

# Dependency graph
npx nx graph
```

## Engineering Principles (mandatory)

Long-term, strategic software engineering is required. A change that works but leaves the code harder to change is not done.

- **Improve the codebase with every feature and bug fix.** Leave the code you touch cleaner than you found it: extract duplication, split oversized files/functions/components, fix misleading names, remove dead code, and add missing tests around what you changed.
- **Fix root causes, not symptoms.** No workarounds or one-off special cases when the underlying design is the problem; fix the design.
- **Stay modular.** Small, focused units with one responsibility and narrow interfaces. Put logic in the right `libs/` layer (see Dependency Constraints) instead of growing app code; keep domain logic out of components and in testable services/stores/pure functions.
- **Clean Code is the standard.** Intention-revealing names, small functions, no magic values, no deep nesting, no copy-paste, single level of abstraction per function, explicit error handling.
- **Easy to maintain beats clever.** Prefer simple, readable code a newcomer can follow over terse or tricky solutions.
- **Scope of cleanup:** improvements to the code your change touches belong in the same PR. A larger refactor that the change exposes but doesn't need goes in its own PR (or an issue), so each PR stays reviewable.

## Coding Rules

1. **Standalone components only** — no NgModules
2. **Zoneless change detection** — never add `zone.js` imports or zone-dependent patterns
3. **Signals for state** — prefer `signal()`/`computed()`/`effect()` over manual subscriptions where possible
4. **OnPush everywhere** — `changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`
5. **Angular Material** — use AM components consistently; don't roll custom UI that AM already covers
   - Exception (pacetrainer): the countdown ring (`pace-countdown-circle`) is a custom SVG, since `mat-progress-spinner` has no track ring
6. **Modern control flow** — `@if`, `@for`, `@switch` (not `*ngIf`, `*ngFor`, `*ngSwitch`)
7. **2-space indentation**, kebab-case filenames, `*.spec.ts` for tests
8. **Explicit `public`/`private`** in class members
9. **Strongly typed** — avoid `any`; use proper generics

## Linting & Formatting

- One workspace-wide `.oxlintrc.json`; there are no per-project lint configs. Add project-specific rules through `overrides` with a `files` glob.
- Type-aware linting is on (`options.typeAware`, backed by `oxlint-tsgolint`). It reads each project's `tsconfig.json` with TypeScript 7 semantics: no `baseUrl`, `paths` relative to `tsconfig.base.json` (`./libs/...`), and no `moduleResolution: node`/`node10`. Keep new tsconfigs on that layout or lint reports `tsconfig-error`.
- `@nx/enforce-module-boundaries` runs inside oxlint through the `@nx/oxlint/boundaries-plugin` bridge; tag constraints live in `.oxlintrc.json`.
- oxlint only lints JS/TS. Angular templates are covered by a second, template-only ESLint setup: the root `eslint.config.mjs` (angular-eslint template rules for `.html` and inline templates, plus the per-project component/directive selector prefixes) is inferred as the `lint-templates` target by `@nx/eslint/plugin`. New Angular projects get their selector prefix added to `selectorPrefixes` in that file. The JSON-based `@nx/dependency-checks` rule is gone; keep package.json deps correct by hand.
- `nx format:write` / `nx format:check` run oxfmt (HTML, SCSS, Markdown and YAML are formatted through its Prettier-backed path).

## Dependency Constraints

```
apps        → features, shared, utils, ui-kit
features    → shared, utils, ui-kit
shared      → utils
utils       → (minimal external deps only)
public      → (own deps only, published packages)
```

Do not create circular dependencies. Run `npx nx graph` to verify.

## Target Policy

- Root `.browserslistrc` and `tsconfig.base.json` govern everything — apps/libs inherit.
- **Do not bump targets in `libs/public/*`** — published packages, held back for consumer compat.
- **`apps/*-cdk` use `target: "ESNext"`** intentionally (Node runtime) — exclude from browser-target changes.

## Native Federation

- `angular-examples` is the shell, remotes are `fourier-analysis-remote`, `bacteria-game-remote`, `shader-examples-remote`.
- Shared setup lives in `tools/federation/workspace-federation.js`; each app's `federation.config.js` only adds its name and `exposes`. A package skipped in one app must be skipped in all of them, or the shell and a remote disagree about the import map. The game lib's secondary entries (`engine`, `admin-kit`, `watch`) are skipped there with the lib.
- `exposes` paths resolve from the workspace root (`./apps/<app>/src/...`), not the project root.
- **Nothing but the exposed module belongs in `src/app/remote-entry/`.** Native Federation maps the whole _directory_ of an exposed file to the remote's public name, so a sibling file imported with a static `import` from outside that folder is rewritten to `<remote>/Routes` and its exports vanish at runtime. That is why each remote's bootstrap component sits in `src/app/`, not next to `entry.routes.ts`.
- A remote also has to run standalone (its own e2e serves it that way), so check both: loaded through the shell _and_ opened on its own port.
- Remotes are listed in `apps/angular-examples/src/assets/federation.manifest.json` (dev) and `federation.manifest.prod.json` (prod).
- Each app has an `esbuild` target (`@angular/build:application`) wrapped by a `build`/`serve` target from `@angular-architects/native-federation`. Change build options on `esbuild`.
- `bacteria-game-remote` runs on Firebase Hosting (`firebase.bacteria-game-remote.json`, site `bacteria-wars`, domain `bacteria-wars.wolsok.de`), deployed by its `deploy` target together with the Firestore and Realtime Database rules. The shell's prod manifest loads the remote from there, and the shell reloads once when a navigation fails on a remote bundle a release replaced (`core/reload-on-stale-bundle.ts`). The old domain `bacteria-game.wolsok.de` is gone; `bacteria-game-remote-cdk` (stack `BacteriaGame`) only holds the new domain's CNAME, whose construct id must stay as it is.
- The game's legal pages live in `bacteria-game-remote`, not the lib: `/privacy` and `/impressum` (`src/app/privacy`, `src/app/impressum`, sharing `src/app/legal/`). Both name the provider from `SITE_OWNER` (`@wolsok/shared-legal`, `libs/shared/legal`: name, email, postal address, VAT ID), shown by its `SiteOwnerComponent` (`<wolsok-site-owner>`), as on RollaPolla's and wolsok.de's `/privacy` and `/impressum`, which also fills `siteOwner` in the support options for the footer's copyright line. The game lib's `support/` folder links to the pages from the footer under the main menu (the route paths are the lib's `legal-links.ts`, used by `app.routes.ts`) and offers the Android app or the PWA in a banner (`InstallOffer`), both only where `provideGameSupport` is set up: on the game's own site, never in the shell.

It takes from the game only `@wolsok/feat-lazy-bac-game/admin-kit`, has texts of its own in English and German, and must stay out of what every visitor loads: the remote's production `build` ends with `tools/bacteria-game/check-lazy-admin.mjs`, which fails when the admin's sources reach `main`, the polyfills or `Routes`.
- Exception: `bacteria-game-remote` is also a standalone PWA. Its federation build is `build-federation`; `build` then reruns `ngsw-config`, since the federation builder writes its files after Angular has hashed the output into `ngsw.json`.
- Error reports go to Sentry (org `wolsok`): the shell to `angular-examples` (`bootstrap.ts`, `core/core.module.ts`), the game to `bacteria-wars`, started only by the remote's standalone `bootstrap.ts` and `app.config.ts` (`src/app/error-reports/`), never by the lib or the exposed routes, and only where the environment has a `sentry` block (`environment.prod.ts`). The SDK is imported dynamically (`import()` in `error-reports.ts`), so it stays off the start's path; errors from before it loaded wait for it. Import it nowhere else but as a type. Errors only and no personal data (owner's decision of 2026-10-26): no tracing, Replay or sessions, `dataCollection.userInfo: false`, and `scrub.ts` drops the user, strips query, hash (`#friend=…`) and id-like tokens, and the attributes of click breadcrumbs (avatars name players in `aria-label` and `alt`). `@sentry/angular` is skipped in `workspace-federation.js`, so each app bundles its own copy. The release is `bacteria-wars@v<version.json>`, created by `.github/actions/create-release`; a change to what is sent goes into the privacy policy (section 10) too.
- Fonts and icons are self-hosted: each app's global `styles.scss` imports the Fontsource faces (latin subsets) and `material-icons/iconfont/filled.css`, and nothing loads from Google Fonts (Angular's font inlining fetched them at build time, which failed the release build, and Google would get every visitor's IP). The shell imports the game's faces too (Atkinson Hyperlegible, Bricolage Grotesque, Cookie), since only the remote's JavaScript reaches it. The game's PWA caches them as `/media/**`.
- `nx serve angular-examples` only serves the shell. Use `nx run angular-examples:serve-all` to boot the shell plus all remotes (ports 4200-4203).

## Cloud Functions (Bacteria Wars)

- `apps/bacteria-wars-functions` is the game's server code (ADR 0011, 0012): 2nd-gen functions, codebase `bacteria` in `firebase.bacteria-game-remote.json`, region `REGION` in `src/config.ts` (the Firestore location of `bacteria-wars`). It takes the engine from `@wolsok/feat-lazy-bac-game/engine` and bundles it (`@nx/esbuild`, ESM, `thirdParty: false`); `firebase-admin` and `firebase-functions` stay external, at the versions in the app's own `package.json`, which a spec keeps equal to the workspace's.
- The client never calls a function: it writes command documents (`replaySubmissions`, `replayCommands`) that triggers process. Triggers run with retries off and are idempotent (`create()` or a transaction checks first).
- The boards (`src/boards/`) are written by functions only: entries carry no uid (`boardMembers/{uid}.entryIds` maps them), `rebuildTop` alone writes a board's top document, and every composite query has its index checked by `indexes.spec.ts` against `firestore.indexes.json`, since the emulator enforces none.
- `test` runs the pure specs; `test-emulator` runs `*.emulator.ts` against the Firestore emulator on ports of its own (`emulator.json`). The game's rules are tested the same way in `apps/bacteria-game-remote/rules-test` (`bacteria-game-remote:test-emulator`). CI runs both targets.
- Errors go to the Sentry project `bacteria-wars-functions` (`src/error-reports.ts`, DSN `SENTRY_DSN` in `src/config.ts`): `main.ts` calls `initErrorReports()`, which starts `@sentry/node` only in a deployed function (`K_SERVICE` set, not the emulator or Jest), and wraps every exported handler in `withSentry(handler)`, which captures, waits for `flush` and rethrows, so retries stay as they were. A new function gets the wrapper too; handler modules stay free of Sentry. `@sentry/node` is external and in the app's `package.json` at the workspace's version (`package-json.spec.ts`).
- Handler modules import `firebase-functions/logger`, not `firebase-functions`: the root export loads the admin auth stack, which Jest on Node 22 cannot require.
- Re-running a replay (`boards/verify.ts`) costs real CPU: `gpu-int`, the only ruleset ranked attempts take, plays at about 7 ms a tick on `IntSimulation`, so a 10-minute match takes minutes. Specs never replay whole matches: `verifyDailySlice` takes the verifier as a parameter, and `verify.spec.ts` mocks `playReplay`. Firestore holds no arrays in arrays; flatten what a function stores.
- `hourly` (`boards/hourly.ts`) is exported only with `HOURLY_ON` in `src/config.ts`; set it to `false` to take it out of a deploy.
- `featureBest` (`gallery/feature-best.ts`, the gallery's daily pick into `publicReplays`) is exported only with `FEATURE_BEST_ON` in `src/config.ts`, on since the gallery's pages and the Replays view of `/admin` shipped (ADR 0011 rollout step 6); set it to `false` to take it out of a deploy.
- Account deletion erases the player's data (ADR 0012, owner's decisions of 2026-10-26) through three `auth.user().onDelete` triggers: `deletePlayerBoards` (`admin/accounts.ts`: boards, bans, audit, count), `deletePlayerData` (`social/delete-player.ts`: `players/{uid}/**`, profile, the player in other players' lists, queue, open rooms, invites, presence and both mirrors) and `deletePlayerReplays`, which no longer deletes replays: `replays/forget.ts` takes the uid out of `players`, seats, `optOut` and `reports`, and the replay stays for the statistics until its `expireAt` (none while still public). It deletes the player's pending `replaySubmissions` and `replayCommands` first; `acceptReplay` reads its submission in its slot and store transactions and drops one that is gone (`withdrawn`), so taking the slot marks the submission (`slotTaken`) rather than deleting it. A new collection keyed by uid, or one that names a uid in a field, gets its erasing there too. Keep `erasePlayer` (`admin/erase.ts`) calling all three parts.
- `guestCleanup` (`admin/guests.ts`, daily at 03:41 UTC) deletes guest accounts (no provider) unused for `GUEST_IDLE_DAYS` (90); exported only with `GUEST_CLEANUP_ON`, on together with the friends-only status rule, which ships only after "Mirror friend lists" (`presence.backfill`) has run once in production. Auth's bulk `deleteUsers` fires no `onDelete`, so it runs `erasePlayer` for each guest first and deletes the account only once that succeeded. It lowers `stats/accounts` once a batch by the decrements its erases claimed (`accountCounted` cleared in a transaction, so each account counts down once), never once a guest.
- The friend lists are mirrored into the Realtime Database by `mirrorFriend` and `mirrorRequest` (`social/mirror.ts`): `statusReaders/{owner}/{reader}` (for the coming friends-only read rule of `status/{owner}`) and `listedBy/{uid}/{owner}/{friends|requests}` (where the deletion finds the player in others' lists). Functions only: the database rules close both to clients. Both triggers retry; each re-reads the entry after its write and writes again if it changed, so out-of-order events end right. Ids the Realtime Database takes as no key (`isRealtimeKey` in `admin/realtime.ts`) are skipped everywhere, and the Firestore rules take only uid-shaped ids in `friends`, `requests` and `challenges`. The admin command `presence.backfill` adds what is missing and removes entries without a list entry.
- The player's replay command `forget` ("Delete" in "My matches", `replays/forget.ts`) takes them out of the replay and its public copies; allowed while banned, like every deletion, and refused (`ranking`) while the boards may still rank the match, an online match still `waiting` for its second report included (`stillRanking` in `replays/forget-plan.ts`).
- Its `deploy` target (`firebase deploy --config=firebase.bacteria-game-remote.json --only functions:bacteria --force`) calls the Firebase CLI itself, not `nx run bacteria-game-remote:firebase`: the game's hosting deploy runs that task in the same release, and the second, nested run of it failed every functions deploy. It runs in the `non-cdk` leg of `deploy.yml` whenever a release affects the app, which includes every change to the game lib (`feat-lazy-bacteria-game`), since the app imports its engine. `--force` deletes functions of the `bacteria` codebase that are gone from `main.ts`, so taking a function out of the exports takes it out of production. The game's hosting deploy leaves the functions alone (`--only hosting,firestore,database`).
- Every Firebase `predeploy` that runs `npm install` for a function (`firebase.bacteria-game-remote.json`, `firebase.pacetrainer.json`, `firebase.rollapolla-analog.json`) passes `--legacy-peer-deps=false`: deploys run inside `npx nx`, which exports the root `.npmrc` as `npm_config_legacy_peer_deps=true`, and the lock written that way lacks required peers, so Cloud Build's `npm ci` refuses it (`Missing: … from lock file`). A spec in each app keeps the flag (`package-json.spec.ts`, `firebase-deploy.spec.ts`); a new function config gets both.

## Android App

- `apps/bacteria-wars-android` is a Gradle project, not a web build: a Trusted Web Activity that opens `https://bacteria-wars.wolsok.de` (the `bacteria-game-remote` PWA) fullscreen in Chrome. Game changes go into the PWA; the app picks them up with the next web deploy.
- Its Nx targets are `apk`, `bundle`, `lint-android` and `deploy`, deliberately not `build`/`lint`/`test`: the Nx Cloud workers have no Android SDK. The `Android app` GitHub workflow (`.github/workflows/android.yml`) builds and lints it on PRs instead. `deploy` signs the release, attaches the APK and bundle to the GitHub release and uploads the bundle to Play's closed testing track (`alpha`); the `android` leg of `deploy.yml` runs it when a release affects the app. See its `README.md` for signing and Play.
- Fullscreen depends on `apps/bacteria-game-remote/src/.well-known/assetlinks.json` naming the app's package and signing-key fingerprints. Gradle reads the package name from that file, so it is the one place to change it; the host is set in `app/build.gradle.kts` and served by Firebase Hosting (`firebase.bacteria-game-remote.json`).
- Launcher icons and splash come from `npx nx run bacteria-game-remote:icons`; don't edit the PNGs by hand.
- `store/` holds what Play shows: the listing texts and graphics, the promo videos and, in `store/play-games/achievements/`, the Play Games Services achievement icons (`npx nx run bacteria-wars-android:achievement-icons`). The achievements themselves are the game's: `play-games-achievements.json` in `libs/features/lazy/bacteria-game/src/lib/state/`, with its spec keeping it in line with the game's achievements. The deploy syncs them to Play as drafts (`tools/bacteria-game/play-games.ts`); the Publish page in Play Console takes them live. Game details and graphics of the Play Games project are the store listing's, entered by hand.
- `app/google-services.json` registers the app with the Firebase project `bacteria-wars` (the `google-services` Gradle plugin, Firebase Analytics, with the advertising id permission removed in the manifest); the Android OAuth client Play Games Services needs lives on that Firebase app. Its `project_number` is also the Play Games Services game id: Gradle puts it into `game_services_project_id` for the manifest's `APP_ID`, the deploy reads it for the achievement sync, and `BacteriaWarsApplication` starts the Play Games SDK, which signs the player in silently on launch. The game itself (in Chrome) cannot reach that SDK; unlocking achievements from the web is still open. The privacy policy (`apps/bacteria-game-remote/src/app/privacy`) names Analytics and the Play Games sign-in; keep it in step with what the app does.
- `tools/bacteria-game/dish.ts` holds the colony palette and the petri dish both icon generators draw with; change colours there.
- Tips and ads live in the game lib's `support/` folder and are switched on by `provideGameSupport` in the remote's app config only, so the shell shows neither. On the web the game links to Buy Me a Coffee; in the app it sells Play tips instead (Play allows no other donation link). Ads come from a network behind the `AdNetwork` port (`support/ads/`, ADR 0017): `GameAds` loads the adapter `support.ads.network` names in `environment.prod.ts` (`adinplay` or `adsense`), whose script brings the network's consent banner; without `support.ads` the game loads no ad script at all, as on the live site until AdinPlay takes it. A new network is an adapter of its own, never a special case in a screen. Keep interstitials and auto ads off, or ads cover the game. The privacy policy's section 7 is rendered per network (`GameAds.networkName`); a new one gets its text there. The shared tip settings are in `environments/game-support.ts`. Changes to them belong into the privacy policy (`src/app/privacy`) too.

## SEO & Sitemaps

**Keep the portfolio in sync, in the same PR as the sitemap.** `apps/portfolio/src/app/projects.ts` lists every app, every `angular-examples` page worth showing (`EXPERIMENTS`) and every published package (`PACKAGES`); a change that adds, renames, removes or noticeably changes one updates its entry too (name, description, tech, links). - **rollapolla-analog**: `/sitemap.xml` is a Nitro route (`src/server/routes/sitemap.xml.ts`, URLs from `src/server/sitemap/sitemap.ts`). Every page sets its tags through `usePageTags` / `useNoindexPage` in `src/app/pages/site-tags.ts`: its own title, description and canonical URL, and `noindex` for personal pages. Unknown pages and missing polls answer 404 (`injectSetNotFoundStatus`). Don't put a static `sitemap.xml` in `src/public`, because Firebase Hosting would serve it instead of the route.
- **angular-examples**: `src/sitemap.xml` is kept by hand. It lists every route in `APP_ROUTES`, or its visible tabs when the route redirects to one, since the canonical URL is the URL after the redirect. Every main route needs a `data.description`. `seo.service.spec.ts` checks both: update it together with the sitemap.
- **portfolio** (`wolsok.de`): prerendered (`outputMode: static`), so each route is a page of its own. `public/sitemap.xml` is kept by hand and lists every route in `app.routes.ts` (`app.component.spec.ts` checks it); each route sets `data.title` and `data.description` in both languages, `SeoService` sets title, canonical and Open Graph tags for the active language. A new project goes into `src/app/projects.ts`. `public/ads.txt` and the AdSense tags in `index.html` belong to AdSense; keep them. `portfolio-cdk` uploads each prerendered page a second time under its bare path, because CloudFront serves no folder index.
  - The site speaks English and German at runtime (`src/app/i18n/`: `I18nService`, `texts.en.ts` with `texts.de.ts` owing it every key, `Localized` values in the data) and is prerendered in English; a German browser switches after hydration, the choice is kept in `localStorage`. The theme (`src/app/theme/`) follows the system through `color-scheme: light dark` and `light-dark()` in `styles.scss`; a choice pins `data-theme`, which a script in `index.html` restores before the first paint.
  - `/privacy` and `/impressum` (`src/app/privacy/`, `src/app/impressum/`, styled by `src/app/legal/legal-page.scss`) are German, the binding version, with a short English one; both name the owner from `SITE_OWNER`.

A monthly scheduled Claude task updates it as `docs/agents/career-update.md` says; `career.spec.ts` checks the data, the build's budgets its size.
- **bacteria-game-remote** (`bacteria-wars.wolsok.de`): `src/sitemap.xml` and `src/robots.txt` are kept by hand and shipped as assets. The sitemap lists the game and every page route in `app.routes.ts` (`sitemap.spec.ts` checks it); the legal pages set their tags through `legal/legal-page.ts`, with the origin from the lib's `GAME_SITE_URL`. The public replay pages (`/replays`, `/replays/{id}`) are no SPA routes: Hosting rewrites `/replays` and `/replays/**` to the `publicSite` function (`apps/bacteria-wars-functions/src/site/`), which renders their tags itself and serves their own sitemap, `/replays/sitemap.xml` (both languages, with `hreflang` alternates), listed in `robots.txt` beside the game's (`site/hosting.spec.ts` checks the rewrites and their cache headers, `sitemap.spec.ts` that line). ## Testing

- **Unit (Jest)**: colocated as `<file>.spec.ts`; mock external services; keep fast and deterministic
- **Unit (Vitest)**: used in Vite-based projects (check `project.json` for the `@nx/vitest` plugin / `@nx/vitest:test` executor)
- **E2E (Playwright)**: in `apps/<app>/e2e/`; page objects in `e2e/pos/`, fixtures in `e2e/fixtures/`
  - Start every `webServer` through an Nx target (`npx nx serve <app>`, `npx nx run <app>:<target>` for a `continuous` target) with `reuseExistingServer: true`. Only then does `@nx/playwright` make the atomized `e2e-ci--*` tasks depend on those servers and wait for them, so several spec files on one Nx Cloud worker share them. A server Playwright starts itself clashes with the next spec file on the same worker (see `rollapolla-analog`). A static server (`@nx/web:file-server`) serves `staticFilePath` and `dependsOn: ["build"]` with `watch: false`, not a `buildTarget`: with `buildTarget` it runs a nested `nx build`, which Nx refuses as a recursive task invocation inside a shared run. Exception for now: `angular-examples` (the federation shell, one spec file) still lets Playwright start its server in CI; with the inferred serve dependency its page did not render on the Nx Cloud workers, while it passed locally.
- **GPU cross-check (Playwright, no server)**: `libs/features/lazy/bacteria-game/playwright.config.ts` runs the deterministic simulation's integer shaders on SwiftShader against the TypeScript reference, tick by tick (`gpu-crosscheck/`, ADR 0015). It is inferred as the lib's `e2e-ci--*` target, so `nx affected` runs it in CI. The goldens in `golden-gpu-int.json` are regenerated whenever the scenarios, the reference or the hash change; a change to what the passes compute also needs a `BALANCE_VERSION` bump, a scenario change does not; `golden.spec.ts` (Jest) recomputes them from the reference. The same check plays whole matches through the game's `GpuSimulation` (`SIM_SCENARIOS`) against `golden-gpu-sim.json`, which `sim-golden.spec.ts` keeps equal to `IntSimulation`, and runs the on-device self-test; its own hashes are `SELF_TEST_GOLDEN` (`state/gpu-int/self-test-golden.ts`, with `GPU_SELF_TEST_VERSION` bumped on every change), kept in step by `self-test-golden.spec.ts`. `golden-replay.spec.ts` keeps a result of `golden-replay.json` per `BALANCE_VERSION` for each ruleset: `cpu` on `BacteriaSimulation`, `gpu-int` on `IntSimulation`
- **Plugin E2E (Jest)**: `apps/nx-aws-cdk-v2-e2e` exercises `@wolsok/nx-aws-cdk-v2` in a generated throwaway workspace. Its target is `e2e` (not `e2e-ci`), so CI does not run it — run `npx nx e2e nx-aws-cdk-v2-e2e` by hand after changing the plugin

- Usage statistics go to GA4 through Firebase Analytics with `@wolsok/shared-analytics` (`libs/shared/analytics`), only with the visitor's opt-in (Consent Mode basic: nothing loads before it; ads, ad personalisation and Google signals always off). What each app measures, the rules and the GA4 setup are in [`docs/analytics.md`](docs/analytics.md); keep its tables in step with the catalogs.
- Each app keeps its events as a typed catalog (`RollaPollaEvents` in rollapolla's `core/analytics/rollapolla-analytics.ts`, `GameEvents` in the game lib's `analytics/game-analytics.ts`) and tracks through `injectRollaPollaAnalytics()` / `injectGameAnalytics()`, which do nothing where analytics doesn't run (server, development, e2e, the shell, specs). ## Performance Gates

Planned and phased in [ADR 0014](docs/adr/0014-performance-gates-in-ci.md); this section says what is in place. Keep it current with each phase.

- **In place, blocking** (phase 1): Angular budgets on the `production` configuration of each Angular app's `esbuild` target (`portfolio`: `build`), measured through the federation build as CI runs it. CI's `build -c=ci` falls back to `production`, so they run on every affected build and block it. Each holds a `baseline` (measured on 2026-10-26, 1 kB = 1000 bytes as Angular counts):
  - `anyScript` (the largest single script, the game's chunk in `bacteria-game-remote`) and `allScript` (all scripts, initial and lazy): warning +5%, error +10%.
  - `initial`: warning +10%, error +20%.
  - `anyComponentStyle` as before (warning 6 kB, error 8 kB in the game's apps), with no warning left: a stylesheet near the limit gives a part of its component a component of its own (the HUD bar `hud-bar.component.ts`, the training's `menu/mission-list.component.ts`) or groups rules it repeats, rather than raising the limit.
  - pacetrainer and rollapolla-analog build with Vite (Analog) and have no Angular budgets.
- **In place, report-only** (phase 2, since 2026-10-27, blocking after two weeks): the `perf` target on `feat-lazy-bacteria-game` runs `tools/perf/engine-bench.mjs`, which bundles `engine.ts` with esbuild and plays fixed replays (the golden replay on `cpu` and `gpu-int`, and `tools/perf/fixtures/expanse-heavy.json`), comparing each one's median time as a ratio to a calibration loop against `tools/perf/engine-baseline.json`: warns above +10%, fails above +20%, asks for a lower baseline below −10%, and fails when a replay plays differently (checksum, ticks, outcome), no longer parses, or the baseline was measured on another Node major than `.nvmrc`'s (V8 optimises differently, so its ratios don't compare). It is cached, runs alone on its worker (`parallelism: false`), takes about 1.5 minutes and writes its table into the job summary. `--report-only` keeps it from failing until the two weeks are over; the baseline holds the CI workers' ratios on Node 24 (they don't carry over between machines, and not even between all CI workers: one run measured 40-50% above the others, so the report names the CPU, and the two weeks decide whether baselines go per CPU model), so a new baseline (a `perf(feat-lazy-bacteria-game): ...` commit of its own, also due when `BALANCE_VERSION` changes the checksums) takes its ratios from the `perf` output of a CI run; `--update` writes the local machine's, useful only for the checksums.
- **In place, report-only** (phase 3, since 2026-10-27): `apps/bacteria-game-remote/e2e/perf.spec.ts` (Chromium only) plays up to 20 s (at least 8) of a campaign match against the computer on the CPU simulation (`?sim=cpu`), with `Math.random` pinned to a seed by an init script, and reports the frame interval (p50, p95, max), long tasks and the engine's time per tick, each also as a ratio to the calibration loop run in the page. The tick time comes from the game's probe (`state/perf-probe.ts`): the spec puts `window.__bacteriaPerfProbe` on the page before it loads, and `GameStateService.advance` times each tick only then; the game never creates it. The table goes to the log (and the job summary where `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` is set), the numbers into the attachment `frame-time.json`; it fails only when nothing was measured. On SwiftShader the frames take about 67 ms and a tick about 2.5 ms: the painting, not the engine, sets the pace there.
- **In place, report-only** (phase 4, since 2026-10-27): Lighthouse CI (`@lhci/cli`) as a `lighthouse` target on `portfolio` (every prerendered route, listed in its `lighthouse.json`, which `app.component.spec.ts` keeps equal to `app.routes.ts`), `angular-examples` (`/`) and `rollapolla-analog` (`/`, `/polls`), each after its `build`, cached, alone on its worker. `tools/perf/lighthouse-run.mjs <app>` runs `lhci autorun` on Playwright's Chrome (`CHROME_PATH` wins where set), with the app's `apps/<app>/lighthouse.json` (what to serve, which pages) and the shared settings it holds itself: 3 runs per page, mobile defaults, warnings only (LCP 2.5 s, TBT 200 ms, CLS 0.1, 1.6 MB), uploaded to temporary public storage in CI (links in the log), `.lighthouseci/` elsewhere. rollapolla's build is Nitro's `firebase` preset, which listens nowhere: `tools/perf/serve-firebase-function.mjs` serves its public folder and hands every other path to the exported function, as Hosting does; its SSR reads the real project's public polls. The public replay pages of the game (a Cloud Function behind Hosting) are not measured yet.
- **Rules**:
  - A failing gate is fixed in the code, not by raising the limit. Raise a budget or baseline only for growth you want, in its own `perf(<project>): ...` commit, with what grew, by how much and why in the PR body. Lower it when a gate reports a gain.
  - Don't compare absolute milliseconds from CI: the Nx Cloud workers are shared and vary. Runtime gates compare against a calibration loop run in the same process.
  - CI has no GPU. A change to the GPU simulation or the GL painters needs a manual check on a real device, noted in the PR.
  - New engine code must stay cheap per tick: online matches, replays, ranked matches and the Cloud Functions' verification all run the CPU simulation.

- **Conventional Commits** enforced by commitlint: `feat(scope): ...`, `fix(scope): ...`, `chore(scope): ...`

- Pre-commit: Husky + lint-staged (runs automatically)
- **Before every commit**:
  1. `npx nx format:write`
  2. `npx nx affected -t lint,lint-templates`
- PR scope: include summary, UI screenshots if visual, linked issue; cleanups of the touched code belong in the PR (see Engineering Principles), larger unrelated refactors get their own PR
- **Always request a CodeRabbit review** after opening a PR: this repo gets no automatic reviews
  (fewer than 10 stars), so comment `@coderabbitai review` on the PR and work through the findings
- **When CodeRabbit and Codex are both rate-limited**, don't wait for them: review the change
  yourself (`/code-review`) and run `/simplify` on it, then fix what they find
- **Merge it yourself once it is done**: `/code-review` and `/simplify` findings applied, every
  review thread answered or resolved, and CI green on the current head. Squash-merge (the
  history on `main` is one commit per PR). A human approval is not part of "done" here

# Claude in Chrome browser automation

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

If the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load every tool you expect to need in ONE ToolSearch call — the select query accepts a comma-separated list — never one call per tool. Start with the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops
